column4: The winds herald mercy, heavy clouds are driven to dead land, water descends, fruits are brought out, and the dead are likewise brought out; this supplies the rain omitted between 87:4 and 87:5 and joins خ ر ج to resurrection and remembrance.
The good land brings forth its growth بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِ while bad land yields only scant growth; following 7:57, it connects Rabb, emergence, and the section's patch-by-patch difference in soil.

Water descends, valleys flow according to measure, and the torrent carries swelling foam which vanishes while what benefits people remains; this is the section's flood-borne غثاء read through the boundary between what passes and what stays.
Water descends from the sky and أَخْرَجْنَا بِهِۦٓ diverse pairs of plants, explicitly filling the section's hidden link from sky to rain to vegetation.
أَخْرَجَ مِنْهَا مَآءَهَا وَمَرْعَىٰهَا places water and pasture in the same act of emergence and is the Quran's closest verbal counterpart to 87:4.
فَجَعَلْنَٰهُمْ غُثَآءً repeats both the transformation verb and غثاء but makes a destroyed people, rather than pasture, the flood-like refuse.

Water descends, runs as springs, brings out plants of varied colors, then the plants wither yellow and are made حُطَامًا; ثُمَّ يَجْعَلُهُۥ and لَذِكْرَىٰ join 87:5's transformation to 87:9's reminder.
The world's life is rain from the sky, mingled vegetation, and finally هَشِيمًا scattered by winds, giving the full Quranic analogue of pasture becoming dry debris.
وَٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ names the enduring counterweight immediately after 18:45's scattered plants, linking the section's ب ق ي family to its fading worldly grass.
Worldly life is vegetation after rain that delights growers, then يَهِيجُ, yellows, and becomes حُطَامًا; the verse directly stages the green-to-dry journey used to expose the lower life's brevity.

Rain makes the earth's vegetation mingle and adorn the land before it is made harvested as though it had not flourished yesterday; the sudden فَجَعَلْنَٰهَا transition expands 87:5's compressed ending.
مُدْهَآمَّتَانِ describes two gardens dark with lush green, supplying the living, luxuriant pole that the section says أَحْوَىٰ can hold beside blackened decay.
لَا يَمُوتُ فِيهَا وَلَا يَحْيَىٰ exactly repeats the condition later voiced in 87:13, setting the plant's clear life-and-death cycle against hell's suspended condition.
Death comes to the punished person from every side وَمَا هُوَ بِمَيِّتٍ, another precise boundary between ordinary dying matter and the person who cannot complete death.

Barren earth receives water, then ٱهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ and grows beautiful pairs; its quivering growth directly matches the section's lexical definition of a living plant and makes that revival an argument for resurrection.

Humbled earth quivers and swells when water descends, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead; this is the same living plant sign and resurrection bridge as the section's journey from dead soil.
Lightning is shown for fear and hope, water descends from the sky, and earth is revived after death, uniting the section's faint cloud-edge flash with the rain called life.

Clouds are driven, joined, and heaped; rain and hail emerge from them, and their lightning nearly takes sight, staging the whole cloud-to-rain movement while contrasting with the section's weak crosswise flash.
A rain cloud contains darkness, thunder, and lightning, supplying a direct Quranic storm setting for the section's first cloud and its marginal flash.

The lightning nearly snatches sight, yet people walk when it lights and stop when darkness returns; this turns watching intermittent nocturnal light into movement and contrasts with the lexicon's weak lightning watched through the night.
Lightning brings fear and hope while heavy clouds are raised, directly joining the flash to the laden cloud and showing a more forceful manifestation than the section's faint one.
Thunder glorifies God with praise while angels do so in awe and thunderbolts are sent; the storm scene itself performs the glorification commanded at the image's opening.

سِيمَاهُمْ marks the believers' faces, and the same ayah compares them to a crop that sends out its shoot, strengthens, and stands firm; it uniquely joins the recorded و س م derivation's mark with visible plant growth.
Water descends from the sky and God brings out every kind of growth, including خَضِرًا from which grain emerges, making green life the explicit product of the omitted rain.

Water from the sky revives earth after death, creatures spread, winds turn, and clouds are controlled between sky and earth; the ayah lays out the section's complete vertical and moving weather system.
Water descends for drink and grows trees فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ, where livestock are sent to graze; rain, plant, pasture, and the act of grazing meet in one verse.
With that water God grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, continuing 16:10's rain-to-grazing scene into the abundance hidden between 87:4 and 87:5.
Water descends from the sky بِقَدَرٍ and is lodged in the earth, joining measured provision to its hidden storage and to the possibility that God can remove it.
Gardens and abundant fruits are produced by the measured, stored water of 23:18, completing its descent-to-growth sequence.
Adjacent plots, gardens, crops, and palms receive one water yet differ in produce, a Quranic counterpart to the section's patchy earth whose growth appears in one place and not another.
Water from the sky brings fruits of varied colors, followed by white, red, and intensely black mountain tracts; it places rain-grown color beside the section's black-over-white خ ر ج color sense.
The king sees seven green ears of grain and others dry, holding fresh and desiccated plant states together just as the section reads both lush darkness and blackened waste through one color image.
The same green and dry ears are repeated when Joseph is asked for their meaning, preserving the explicit juxtaposition of a plant's two ends in the interpretive scene.
The question “Have you seen what you sow?” opens a compact sequence about human planting, divine growth, and possible reduction to debris that closely parallels 87:4–5.
The ayah asks whether people make the crop grow or God does, making the divine agency behind “He brought out the pasture” explicit.
God could make the crop حُطَامًا, directly matching the pasture's divinely caused conversion into dry wreckage.
The sequence turns from crop to the water people drink, bringing the otherwise omitted water into the same act of contemplating provision.
The question asks whether people sent water down from ٱلْمُزْنِ, the rain clouds, or God did, naming the cloud source that the section reconstructs behind the pasture.
فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ concludes the sowing, rain-cloud, and water sequence with the same command to glorify the Lord's name that opens surah 87.
Blessed water descends from the sky and produces gardens and harvest grain, presenting rain as the life-bearing provision behind emergence.
The water is provision, revives a dead land, and ends كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ, explicitly turning plant emergence into the pattern of resurrection.
Profuse water descends from rain clouds, naming the cloud-to-rain step developed in the section.
Grain and vegetation are brought out by that rain, supplying the next link in the vertical chain.
Dense gardens complete the rain sequence with dark abundance, the living visual pole opposite the later black refuse.
أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَآءَ صَبًّا makes the poured rain the first explicit stage in the Quran's close analysis of human food.
ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّا shows the earth split for emergence, making concrete the section's claim that growth is pulled out from a place.
Fruit and أَبًّا, pasture or fodder, are the end products of the poured water and split earth, directly meeting المرعى's plant-and-feed sense.
The whole rain-to-growth sequence is provision for people and their livestock, completing pasture as a relation between plant, animal, and provider.
The oath by the sky “of return” evokes returning rain from above, the repeated descent behind the pasture's emergence.
The paired oath by the splitting earth supplies the cracked ground through which the hidden plant is brought out.
A sign is the dead earth: God gives it life and brings grain out of it, compressing death, revival, and concrete emergence into one agricultural scene.
Water descends from the sky in measure, revives a dead land, and is followed by كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ, joining measured rain to human emergence.
Winds raise clouds, clouds are driven to dead land, and earth is revived; كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ makes the exact cloud-rain-life movement a resurrection sign.
Water is driven to barren land and brings out crops eaten by livestock and people, directly uniting the moving cloud-water system with pasture and provision.
The Creator sends water from the sky and grows flourishing gardens that humans could not grow, reinforcing the divine subject behind pasture's emergence.
Winds are sent as heralds before mercy and pure water descends from the sky, repeating the cloud system that supplies the missing rain.
That water revives dead land and gives drink to cattle and people, linking the rain called life to creatures sustained by it.
Winds raise clouds, God spreads or fragments them, and rain is seen emerging from within, closely staging the section's first appearing and lingering cloud.
The reader is told to look at the effects of divine mercy in earth's revival after death and infer the revival of the dead, exactly the interpretive move made from living grass.
Water from the sky gives earth life after its death, stating the life-giving role that explains why the section's lexicon can call rain “life.”
Water descends and the earth becomes مُخْضَرَّةً, giving the immediate green mark left on soil by the first rain.
Water from the sky causes every noble kind to grow, another direct statement of the rain-to-emergence link compressed out of 87:4.
Earth is made a resting place, sky a canopy, water descends, and fruits are brought out as provision; it renders the section's sky-to-earth vertical column in one ayah.
God knows the falling leaf, the grain hidden in earth's darkness, and every moist and dry thing; hiddenness, plant location, and the wet-to-dry poles of the image meet under divine knowledge.
God splits grain and seed-stone and brings living from dead and dead from living, expressing both concrete plant emergence and the reversible life/death relation behind the pasture.
Moses identifies “our Lord” as the one who gave each thing its creation and then guided it, repeating the creation-and-guidance order that precedes the pasture in surah 87.
“Eat and pasture your livestock” makes plant growth from 20:53 into both human food and the act of grazing, unpacking المرعى's combined senses.
The زَهْرَةَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا is temporary display, while the Lord's provision is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ; the flower image and exact lasting comparison join the grass cycle to 87:16–17.
What people possess runs out while مَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍ, stating in abstract terms the same passing-versus-remaining boundary shown by grass and enduring good.
A garden on high ground bears doubled produce under heavy rain and still yields under light rain, showing how differing rain intensities nourish rather than merely accompany the green mark.
All things have their treasuries with God and descend only in known measure, framing the rain in 15:22 as hidden, measured provision.
Fertilizing winds are sent, water descends from the sky, and people are not its storekeepers, directly linking moving air, rain, life, and provision beyond human control.
God's reviving of earth after its death is itself an explained sign, the same perceptible transition the section sees in fresh moving plants.
Water descends from the sky and fruits are brought out as provision, restating the core vertical movement from above to emerged food.
Water from the sky revives earth after death, and the expected confession that God did it preserves the divine agency central to 87:4.
Provision descends from the sky, revives earth after death, and is named beside the turning winds, joining sustenance, life, and moving air.
The sky is promised as abundant rain, using the upper covering itself as the source of the water developed in the section's س م و family.
That rain supplies wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, completing its role as sustained provision and growth.
The command to look at earth and how many noble pairs God has caused to grow directs attention to the same visible act of pasture emerging.
Earth's contents are made an adornment and a test, giving the flourishing first half of the image whose removal follows in 18:8.
Earth's adornment is destined to become barren ground, a direct large-scale counterpart to green pasture becoming lifeless refuse.
Two fertile gardens and the command to eat the Lord's provision display the sweet, nourished state before the flood reversal in 34:16.
The people of the Fire are not finished by death and their punishment is not lightened, extending the boundary expressed by “neither dies nor lives.”
A downpour strikes thin soil on rock and leaves it bare, reversing the section's first rain that marks earth with vegetation.
A bitterly cold wind strikes and destroys a crop, setting destructive weather against the cloud and rain that nourish pasture.
The promised garden has enduring fruit and shade, the precise vegetal opposite of pasture whose taste, greenness, and body are carried away.
The good word is a good tree with firm root and branch in the sky, answering the section's short-lived grass with stability across the same earth-to-sky axis.
The tree gives fruit in every season بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهَا, directly opposing the summer-withering pasture and bringing Rabb into enduring growth.
The bad word is an uprooted tree with no stability, marking the boundary on the other side of the enduring tree and resembling vegetation reduced to unattached debris.
The punishment of the Day of the Canopy turns an overhead cloud-like shade from shelter and promised rain into destruction.
A sent wind makes the crop yellow and people become ungrateful, reversing the life-bearing wind and rain of 30:48–50.
The dam flood replaces two fruitful gardens with bitter fruit and sparse trees, combining destructive water, lost sweetness, and ruined vegetation.
Fire is produced from a green tree, making living greenness and burning meet at a boundary that sharpens the section's later fire/life opposition.
A cloud appearing over the valleys is welcomed as rain, but is identified as the hastened punishment bearing a painful wind; first appearance and expected rain are decisively reversed.
The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command, showing what a cloud-driven wind can leave when it bears devastation instead of pasture-making rain.
The wind sent to ʿĀd is explicitly barren, the opposite of the fertilizing, rain-bearing air in the section's weather column.
That wind leaves whatever it passes like decayed matter, reaching the same wrecked endpoint as غثاء without the intervening green life.
God could make the rain-cloud water bitter, a boundary that answers both drinkable rain and the section's pasture losing its sweetness.
If water sinks away, no one can bring flowing water back; this makes the normally hidden provision perceptible through its possible withdrawal.
سَنَسِمُهُ عَلَى ٱلْخُرْطُومِ uses branding as punitive exposure, contrasting with the recorded و س م derivation in which first rain marks earth by making green growth visible.
The garden becomes like a stripped or blackened field overnight, a sudden dark endpoint that illuminates أَحْوَىٰ as decayed blackness rather than lush dark green.
Pharaoh's “I am your lord, the most high” usurps the exact رب/أعلى relation of 87:1, clarifying by reversal whose name the command to glorify bears.
The people of the Fire have only a harsh dry plant for food, turning vegetation from life-giving pasture into part of punishment.
That plant neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, a sharp reversal of the pasture and rain whose very names carry feeding and life.
Clouds shade the people from above, directly exemplifying the section's definition of sky as whatever rises over and shades a person, though no rain falls here.
The cloud again shades a people, repeating the overhead-covering sense developed from س م و while the surrounding passage supplies water and food by other means.
The she-camel is to be left to eat on God's earth, a concrete animal-side realization of المرعى as grazing, though the verse does not show the grass's growth.
Earth is spread and every measured thing is caused to grow in it, joining vegetation to the section's preceding idea of divine measure.
The varied colors of what God has multiplied on earth provide a wider palette for the section's attention to green, yellow, and black plant states.
Pharaoh's question “Who is your Lord, Moses?” makes the رب in 20:50's creation-and-guidance answer an explicit point of dispute.
Humans are created from earth, returned to it, and brought out from it again, extending the plant emergence of 20:53 into the same resurrection pattern.
Every living thing is made from water, supporting the lexical claim that rain is called “life,” although this ayah speaks of water generally rather than pasture.
A people's sheep graze through a cultivated field at night, realizing grazing as an action while showing it as damage to another person's growth.
The crowd watering flocks and the two women holding theirs back place herd, herders, and water together, a social counterpart to pasture's grass-place-grazing complex.
People, creatures, and livestock have varied colors, extending 35:27's black, white, and red landscape colors to animals and recalling the section's camel-color definition of أَحْوَىٰ.
Rain descends after despair and mercy is spread, fitting the section's first life-giving rain though the ayah leaves vegetation unstated.
Earth splits from the resurrected as they emerge swiftly, completing the literal human خروج anticipated by the rain-and-revival image at 50:11.
A destroyed people become like dry stalks used by a pen-builder, another transfer of plant wreckage imagery to human ruin comparable to 23:41.
Everything is created according to measure, a concise Quranic parallel to the measured ordering that precedes pasture in surah 87.
فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ repeats the command-object formula of 87:1 and helps keep “name” and “Lord” as their primary meanings beneath the section's family imagery.
The same command to glorify the name of the Magnificent Lord closes another surah, confirming the worship formula echoed at 87:1.
Sweet water is given to drink, a direct positive pole for the section's mention of sweetness lost when floodwater turns pasture into debris.
Water and pasture in 79:31 are declared provision for people and livestock, spelling out the feeding relation contained in المرعى.
The command that a person look at their food establishes the contemplative stance for the rain, cracked earth, vegetation, and pasture that follow.
Grain is the first named growth from poured water and split earth, marking the concrete emergence stage.
Grapes and herbage continue the fresh plant abundance before the passage arrives at explicit fodder.
Olive and palm extend the varieties drawn out of the cracked earth by rain.
Dense gardens supply the lush dark-green visual pole immediately before fruit and pasture are named.
God creates everything and determines it with exact measure, paralleling the creation-and-measure order that frames the pasture image without itself naming vegetation.
Worldly enjoyment and adornment are set against what is with God as better and more lasting, stating the same comparison the fading pasture makes visible.
Provision is sent down from the sky and only one who turns back remembers, linking unnamed heavenly provision to the section's omitted rain and its movement toward reminder.
A visitation circles the garden while its owners sleep, supplying the unseen cause for the blackened or stripped result stated in 68:20.
Earth brings out its burdens, a non-botanical but strongly concrete instance of إخراج from a containing place that clarifies how literally the section pictures grass being drawn from soil.
The defeated army becomes like eaten straw, another human catastrophe rendered as plant refuse and thus a close thematic cousin of people made غثاء in 23:41.

Moses sees a distant fire at night and asks his family to remain while he seeks a brand or guidance; this may echo the section's lexical night-watcher scanning for lightning, though the light is fire rather than lightning.
Moses' sight of a distant fire and hope for news or a burning brand is a plausible nonlexical parallel to watching a remote nocturnal flash, but the ayah does not involve cloud or rain.

Moses sees fire from the side of the mountain while traveling at night and goes toward it for news or warmth; the connection is limited to the section's secondary scene of sustained attention to light in darkness.

People emerge from graves like scattered locusts; this may faintly parallel rain forcing hidden creatures from holes and the section's concrete خ ر ج imagery, but neither rain nor mice appears in the ayah.
